description: IEEE FIU Nasa Space Apps Team
summary: Crew Context Monitor (CCM) is a health monitoring system that determines whether a change in an astronaut’s vitals originates from the individual or from the cabin environment. A wearable measures pulse, SpO2, skin temperature and motion, while a cabin node measures CO2, temperature, humidity, VOC, particulates and radiation counts. A Raspberry Pi gateway runs fully offline, builds a baseline for each crew member, detects sudden anomalies and slow drift, and correlates cabin readings with physiology. Results appear on a dashboard as four risk cards (cardiovascular, air quality, thermal, radiation), each with a severity color, an attribution (cabin, individual or unclear) and a recommended action. On long missions such as a Mars transit, communication delays and blackouts remove real-time medical support from Earth, so CCM lets the crew catch health changes themselves. Comparing each astronaut to their own history rather than a population norm reduces false alarms, such as an elevated heart rate during exercise. Attribution directs the response to the right place: fixing a scrubber when the cabin is the cause, or resting and remeasuring when it is the individual. Astronauts also control what health data is sent to Earth. CCM is a decision-support prototype, not a medical device.
details:
What it does and how it works

Crew Context Monitor (CCM) determines whether a change in an astronaut’s vitals originates from the individual or from the cabin environment. A wearable measures pulse, SpO2, skin temperature and motion. A cabin node measures CO2, temperature, humidity, VOC, particulates and radiation counts. A Raspberry Pi gateway runs fully offline on its own hotspot, stores both data streams, builds a baseline for each crew member, detects sudden anomalies and slow drift, and correlates cabin readings with physiology. A dashboard shows four risk cards (cardiovascular, air quality, thermal, radiation), each with a severity color, an attribution (cabin, individual or unclear) and a recommended action.

Benefits and intended impact

On long missions such as a Mars transit, communication delays and blackouts remove real-time medical support from Earth. CCM lets the crew catch health changes themselves and directs the response to the right place: fixing a scrubber when the cabin is the cause, or resting and remeasuring when it is the individual. Comparing each astronaut to their own history rather than a population norm reduces false alarms. Health summaries are sent to Earth only after crew approval.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Hardware: Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3, ESP32 dev board, Raspberry Pi; MAX30102, TMP117, MPU6050, SCD41, SGP40, PMS5003 and Geiger counter sensors; 3D-printed PETG enclosures.

Firmware: C++ (Arduino, ESP32 core).

Gateway: Python (FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, paho-mqtt, bleak), Mosquitto MQTT, SQLite.

Dashboard: React, Vite, Recharts, Tailwind.

Design and data: CadQuery for enclosures; WESAD and NASA OSDR datasets.

Creativity

Fuses wearable and cabin data to explain why a vital changed, where a wearable alone only reports that it changed.

Compares crew members against each other to separate a cabin-wide cause from an individual one.

Models expected heart rate from activity, so exercise does not trigger an alarm.

Uses a statistical test on radiation counts instead of a fixed threshold.

Includes a simulator that sends the same messages as the hardware, so mission scenarios such as a scrubber failure or solar particle event can be replayed.

Factors considered

Operation with no link to Earth.

False alarms and alert fatigue.

Sensor noise: pulse sensor placed on the finger, heart-rate variability excluded during motion.

Crew privacy and control over their data.

Honest framing: wording says “consistent with”, never “caused by”, and every screen is labeled as a decision-support prototype, not a medical device.

CO2 thresholds checked against NASA-STD-3001.

Electrical and battery safety.

Fallback to simulated data if a sensor fails.

This is drawn from the plan documents, so adjust anything that changed during the build. In particular, confirm whether the wearable ended up sending over BLE or WiFi, and whether every sensor listed made it into the final hardware.
